title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
The page finishes §14 and gives §15. Setting: Z is a function of x, y and p=dy/dx, q=d²y/dx², r=d³y/dx³, s=d⁴y/dx⁴, …, with dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp + Q dq + R dr + S ds + …. Euler embeds the extremal y(x) in a one-parameter family y(x,t). The variation of the functional J = ∫Z dx is then dt·∂J/∂t, and Lagrange's δy becomes (∂y/∂t)dt. Differentiating under the integral gives

dt∫dx[N y_t + P y_{xt} + Q y_{xxt} + R y_{xxxt} + S y_{xxxxt} + …].

On the previous page he integrated each term repeatedly by parts in x, using the fact that ∂_x(∂^k y/∂x^{k-1}∂t) = ∂^{k+1}y/∂x^k∂t. Collecting the results, the variation splits into two parts.

1. An integral part, all multiplied by y_t:
dt∫dx y_t (N − P' + Q'' − R''' + S'''' − …).

2. Absolute (boundary) parts, each multiplied by a higher mixed derivative:
- y_t multiplied by (P − Q' + R'' − S''' …);
- y_{xt} multiplied by (Q − R' + S'' − …);
- y_{xxt} multiplied by (R − S' + …);
- y_{xxxt} multiplied by (S − …);
- and so on.

§15: Euler says that for the variation to vanish however t enters, the integral part must vanish separately. This is the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations, used tacitly without proof. Once t is dropped, this gives the Euler–Poisson equation for higher-order functionals:

0 = N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − d³R/dx³ + d⁴S/dx⁴ − ….

The boundary 'clausulae' are deferred to the endpoint conditions treated 'alibi' (the Methodus inveniendi of 1744 and the 1760s papers). The purpose is to recover the known one-variable theory with the new auxiliary-parameter device. This prepares §16 onward, where Euler extends the method to functions of two variables (surfaces z(x,y)), a task he says he could not manage in his earlier variational dissertation.
errors: No mathematical error: the coefficients of the boundary terms and of the integrand check out against the integration-by-parts formulas on p.42.
Printing slips: in the first line the derivative of R is printed with a malformed exponent ('d^b R'). In the first equation of §15 the R-term reads d³R/dx² where dx³ is intended.

Logical gap (standard for the period): the step from 'the variation vanishes for every way t enters' to 'the integrand vanishes' assumes the fundamental lemma without justification. It also ignores the interplay with boundary terms, which Euler simply sets aside.

ideas.what: Interpreting the variation δ as differentiation with respect to an auxiliary parameter t of a family y(x,t), δy=(∂y/∂t)dt
ideas.modern_name: one-parameter variation / first variation as derivative d/dε J[y+εη]
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (Novi Comm. Petrop. 16, 1772); the theme is discussed in standard histories (Goldstine, A History of the Calculus of Variations; Fraser)

ideas.what: Repeated integration by parts yielding the higher-order Euler–Lagrange equation plus boundary terms
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Poisson equation and the natural boundary terms of the first variation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi 1744); Lagrange 1760; boundary terms Lagrange/Poisson

ideas.what: Integral part must vanish separately for arbitrary variation
ideas.modern_name: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations (du Bois-Reymond lemma)
ideas.usually_credited_to: used implicitly by Euler/Lagrange; rigorous proof du Bois-Reymond 1879
ideas.where_published: implicit throughout Euler's and Lagrange's variational work

deep.surprise_reason: This is a standard, well-known derivation in a well-studied paper. The parameter-t interpretation of δ in E420 is already documented in the histories of the calculus of variations.
